JDK vs JRE vs JVM?

- JVM: the abstract machine that runs bytecode. It's platform-specific, and that's what makes Java "write once, run anywhere".
- JRE: the JVM plus the core libraries, i.e. what you need to run Java.
- JDK: the JRE plus development tools (javac, jar, jdb, jshell), i.e. what you need to develop Java. (Since Java 11 there's no separate JRE download.)
What are the four pillars of OOP?

- Encapsulation: keep data private and expose it through methods (getters and setters, validation).
- Inheritance: an IS-A relationship (extends) used to reuse code. Java supports only single inheritance of classes.
- Polymorphism: compile-time (method overloading) and runtime (method overriding, resolved by dynamic dispatch).
- Abstraction: hide the implementation and show only the essentials, using abstract classes and interfaces.

Why is String immutable? What is the String pool?

A String can't change once it's created. That gives you:
- A safe String Constant Pool: literals are shared across the app.
- Security: values like file paths, URLs and DB credentials can't be changed after they're checked.
- Thread-safety without synchronization.
- A cached hashCode, which makes Strings good HashMap keys.
String a = "hi";            // pool
String b = "hi";            // same pool object → a == b is true
String c = new String("hi"); // new heap object → a == c is false
c.intern() == a;            // true
String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?

| String | StringBuilder | StringBuffer
Mutable | No | Yes | Yes
Thread-safe | Yes (immutable) | No | Yes (synchronized)
Speed | Slow for concatenation in loops | Fastest | Slower
final vs finally vs finalize?

- final: a variable can't be reassigned, a method can't be overridden, a class can't be extended.
- finally: a block that always runs after try/catch (unless System.exit is called or the JVM crashes). Used for cleanup.
- finalize(): called by the GC before collecting an object. Deprecated since Java 9. Use try-with-resources or Cleaner instead.
Checked vs unchecked exceptions? Show the hierarchy.

Throwable
 ├── Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) – don't catch
 └── Exception
      ├── IOException, SQLException …      → CHECKED (must handle/declare)
      └── RuntimeException                  → UNCHECKED
           ├── NullPointerException
           ├── IllegalArgumentException
           └── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Checked exceptions are verified at compile time. Unchecked exceptions usually mean a programming bug. Spring's @Transactional rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default.
Overloading vs overriding?

Overloading | Overriding
Same method name, different parameters | Same signature in a subclass
Compile-time (static) polymorphism | Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism
Return type can differ | Same return type or a covariant one
Can be in the same class | Needs inheritance; can't override static, final or private methods
Any access modifier | Can't reduce visibility or throw broader checked exceptions

Abstract class | Interface
Can have state (instance fields) and constructors | Only public static final constants
A class can extend only one | A class can implement many
Any access modifiers | Methods are public by default; default, static (Java 8) and private (Java 9) methods allowed
Use for an IS-A base with shared code | Use for a capability or contract (CAN-DO)
How does HashMap work internally?

- put(k,v) calls k.hashCode() and spreads the bits (h ^ (h >>> 16)).
- The index is (n-1) & hash, which is why the capacity is always a power of 2.
- If the bucket is empty, a new Node is stored there. Otherwise the existing nodes are compared with equals(): a match replaces the value, no match appends a node.
- When a 9th node is added to a bucket that already holds 8, the list is converted to a Red-Black tree if capacity is at least 64; below 64 the table resizes instead (Java 8). It converts back to a list at 6.
- When size exceeds capacity × load factor (0.75), the table doubles in size and entries are redistributed.
💡 Keys should be immutable. If a key's hashCode changes while it's in the map, you can't find the entry again.
HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronizedMap?

- HashMap: not synchronized; allows one null key and many null values.
- Hashtable: legacy; every method is synchronized (one lock for the whole table); no nulls.
- Collections.synchronizedMap: a wrapper with a single lock.
- ConcurrentHashMap: Java 8+ uses CAS plus synchronized on the bucket's first node, so reads don't lock. No null keys or values. Its iterators are fail-safe (weakly consistent). It provides atomic computeIfAbsent and merge.
ArrayList vs LinkedList?

ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array: O(1) random access, it grows by 1.5×, and inserting in the middle is O(n). LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(n) access, O(1) insert or remove at the ends or at an iterator position, and it uses more memory per node. ArrayList is the better choice in almost every case, partly because it's cache-friendly.
Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators?

Fail-fast iterators (ArrayList, HashMap) throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified during iteration. They detect this with a modCount check. Use iterator.remove() or removeIf() instead.
Fail-safe iterators (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap) work on a snapshot or are weakly consistent, so they never throw.

What is a functional interface? Can it have default methods?

An interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM). @FunctionalInterface is optional but makes the compiler enforce it. It can also have any number of default and static methods. Examples: Runnable, Callable, Comparator.
Optional — why and how?

Avoids NPEs by modeling "might be absent" explicitly. Use it as a return type, not for fields or parameters.
String city = repo.findById(id)
    .map(User::getAddress).map(Address::getCity)
    .orElse("Unknown");          // orElseGet(supplier), orElseThrow()
Runnable vs Callable; Thread vs ExecutorService?
synchronized vs volatile vs Atomic vs Lock?

- volatile: guarantees visibility (a write happens-before every later read of that variable, enforced with memory barriers). It does not make operations atomic: count++ is still unsafe.
- synchronized: gives both mutual exclusion and visibility. It's reentrant and uses the intrinsic monitor lock.
- AtomicInteger etc.: lock-free CAS for single variables.
- ReentrantLock: like synchronized but adds tryLock, timeouts, fairness, interruptible locking, and multiple Conditions. You must call unlock() in finally.
What is deadlock? How to prevent it?

Two or more threads each hold a lock and wait for a lock the other holds, so none can proceed. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Prevent it by always acquiring locks in the same order, using tryLock with a timeout, keeping locks small, and avoiding nested locks. Use a thread dump (jstack) to detect it.
wait() vs sleep()?

wait() is an Object method. It must be called inside synchronized, it releases the lock, and it's woken by notify or notifyAll. sleep() is a Thread static method. It keeps the lock, can be called anywhere, and wakes after a fixed time.
How does Garbage Collection work? Name the collectors.

The GC finds objects that can't be reached from GC roots (stack locals, static fields, active threads, JNI refs), then marks, sweeps and compacts. Collection is generational: minor GCs in Young, major GCs in Old.
Collectors: Serial, Parallel (throughput), G1 (default since Java 9; region-based, predictable pauses), ZGC (sub-millisecond pauses) and Shenandoah (pauses of a few milliseconds), both for large heaps. System.gc() is only a request.
Can Java have memory leaks? Give examples.

Yes: objects that are still reachable but no longer needed. Examples: static collections that keep growing, unclosed resources, listeners that are never deregistered, ThreadLocal in thread pools that's never removed, inner classes holding a reference to the outer class, and mutable HashMap keys. Diagnose with a heap dump in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM.
How to create an immutable class?

- Declare the class final.
- Make all fields private final.
- Don't provide setters.
- Initialize everything in the constructor and deep-copy mutable inputs.
- Return copies (or unmodifiable views) of mutable fields from getters.
Since Java 16, record gives you shallow immutability for free.
Write a thread-safe Singleton.
Serialization; what does transient do?

Serialization turns an object into a byte stream (implements Serializable, ObjectOutputStream). transient fields are skipped and get their default value back on deserialization. Declare a serialVersionUID to control version compatibility. Static fields aren't serialized.
Java 11 → 17 → 21 features you should know?
What are the SOLID principles?

- Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change.
- Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification.
- Liskov Substitution: a subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is.
- Interface Segregation: prefer small, focused interfaces.
- Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. This is what Spring DI is built on.
Common design patterns asked in Java interviews?

- Creational: Singleton, Factory, Abstract Factory, Builder (Lombok @Builder), Prototype.
- Structural: Adapter, Decorator (Java IO streams), Proxy (Spring AOP), Facade.
- Behavioral: Strategy (Comparator), Observer (event listeners), Template Method (JdbcTemplate), Chain of Responsibility (servlet filters), Command.
Pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value being copied is the reference. A method can change the object's state through that copy, but reassigning the parameter has no effect on the caller.
What does the static keyword mean on a variable, method, block and nested class?

static means the member belongs to the class, not to an instance.
- Variable: one copy shared by all instances, stored with the class.
- Method: called without an object. It has no this, so it cannot touch instance members directly. Static methods are hidden, not overridden.
- Block: runs once, when the class is initialized.
- Nested class: holds no reference to an outer instance.
💡 Mutable static state is shared across all threads and requests, so it is a common cause of concurrency bugs and memory leaks.
Explain the four access modifiers.

Modifier | Class | Package | Subclass (other package) | Everywhere
private | Yes | No | No | No
(default, package-private) | Yes | Yes | No | No
protected | Yes | Yes | Yes, through inheritance | No
public | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes
A top-level class can only be public or package-private. Start with the most restrictive modifier that works. With JPMS modules, even a public type is visible outside its module only if its package is exports-ed.
What is the class-loader delegation model, and why does it exist?

When a class loader is asked for a class, it first delegates to its parent: Application → Platform → Bootstrap. It loads the class itself only if the parent cannot find it. This means core classes such as java.lang.String always come from the bootstrap loader, so application code cannot replace them, and every class is loaded only once per loader. A class's identity is its name plus its defining loader. That is why the same class loaded by two loaders can produce ClassCastException: X cannot be cast to X in app servers and with hot reload.
What is the JIT compiler, and why can Java be as fast as C++ for long-running services?

The JVM first interprets bytecode while it profiles the code. Hot methods are compiled to native code by C1 (fast compile, light optimization) and then by C2 (aggressive optimization). This is called tiered compilation. Because the JIT works from runtime profiles, it can inline virtual calls, remove unneeded locks, use escape analysis and unroll loops. A static compiler cannot always do this. The cost is warm-up: the first requests are slower. For startup-sensitive workloads such as serverless, options include CDS/AOT caches or GraalVM native images.
What are wrapper classes and autoboxing? What is the Integer cache?

Each primitive type has a wrapper class (int→Integer, and so on). Wrappers are needed for generics and collections, and they can be null. Autoboxing converts a primitive to its wrapper automatically (Integer.valueOf). Unboxing goes the other way (intValue()), and it throws NPE on null. Integer.valueOf caches values from -128 to 127, so == between two boxed 127s is true and between two 128s is false. Always compare wrappers with equals.
Integer a = 127, b = 127;   // a == b → true (cached)
Integer c = 128, d = 128;   // c == d → false (two objects)
c.equals(d);                // true

Virtual threads vs platform threads: what changed in Java 21?

A platform thread wraps an OS thread. It is expensive (around 1 MB of stack, kernel scheduling), so apps pool a few hundred of them. A virtual thread is scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. When it blocks on I/O, it unmounts, which frees the carrier, so you can run millions of them. Use them for blocking, I/O-bound code in the thread-per-request style: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), or spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true in Spring Boot 3.2+.
- Do not pool them. Create one per task.
- They do not speed up CPU-bound work.
- Be careful with ThreadLocal-heavy code and with limited downstream resources such as DB connection pools.
- In Java 21, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier. JDK 24 (JEP 491) largely removed that limitation.
Marker interface vs annotation: which should you use?

A marker interface, such as Serializable or Cloneable, has no methods. It defines a type, so the compiler can enforce it, for example void save(Serializable s). An annotation, such as @Entity or @Transactional, carries metadata that frameworks read through reflection. It can have attributes and can be applied to methods, fields and parameters as well as types. Use a marker interface when you want compile-time type checking. Use an annotation for framework metadata or for anything that is not a class.
Strong vs soft vs weak vs phantom references: when is each object collected?

| Strong | Soft | Weak | Phantom
Created by | Normal assignment | SoftReference | WeakReference | PhantomReference (needs a queue)
Collected when | Never, while reachable | Memory is low; always before an OutOfMemoryError | At the next GC once only weakly reachable | After the object is unreachable; the reference is then enqueued
get() | n/a | Object or null | Object or null | Always null
Typical use | Everything | Memory-sensitive caches | WeakHashMap, listeners, canonical maps | Cleanup after death (Cleaner uses it)
Rule of thumb: use weak references when the entry should die with its key, and phantom references (through java.lang.ref.Cleaner) for native-resource cleanup. For caches, a bounded library cache such as Caffeine is more predictable than soft references, which the GC clears in bulk under pressure.
Future vs CompletableFuture: what does CompletableFuture add?

| Future | CompletableFuture
Getting the result | Blocking get() only | get(), join(), or callbacks
Chaining | None | thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine
Combining many | Loop and call get() on each | allOf, anyOf
Error handling | ExecutionException from get() | exceptionally, handle, whenComplete
Completing by hand | Not possible | complete(v), completeExceptionally(e)
Default thread pool | Whatever executor you submitted to | ForkJoinPool.commonPool() for *Async methods without an executor
CompletableFuture<Patient> p = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> repo.find(id), ioPool);
CompletableFuture<List<Lab>> l = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> labs.forPatient(id), ioPool);
Chart chart = p.thenCombine(l, Chart::new).join();
Interview tip: pass your own executor for blocking I/O, because the common pool is small and shared. Also note that cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture does not interrupt the running task.
Class.forName vs ClassLoader.loadClass: what is the difference?

| Class.forName(name) | loader.loadClass(name)
Runs static initializers | Yes, by default | No (load only; initialization waits for first use)
Which loader | The caller's class loader | The loader you call it on
Control | forName(name, initialize, loader) lets you choose both | Fixed: no initialization
Classic use | Old JDBC driver registration (static block registers the driver) | Frameworks and plugins that scan classes without side effects
Rule of thumb: use forName when you need the class ready to use, and loadClass when you only want to inspect it. Since JDBC 4, drivers register through ServiceLoader, so Class.forName("com.mysql...Driver") is no longer needed.
Date and Calendar vs LocalDateTime vs Instant vs ZonedDateTime: which do you use?

| Date / Calendar | LocalDate(Time) | Instant | ZonedDateTime / OffsetDateTime
Meaning | An instant, shown in the default zone | Wall-clock date or time, no zone | A point on the UTC timeline | Date-time with a zone (DST rules) or a fixed offset
Mutable | Yes | No | No | No
Thread-safe | No (and SimpleDateFormat is not either) | Yes | Yes | Yes
Good for | Legacy APIs only | Birth dates, opening hours | Audit timestamps, event times | Appointments in a user's zone, API payloads
Rule of thumb: store and compare moments as Instant (in UTC), keep a date of birth as LocalDate, and convert to ZonedDateTime only for display or for scheduling in a specific zone. Format with DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable and thread-safe.
